paras: The Braswell trestle lynching was the hanging of an unnamed Black man from a railroad trestle at Braswell, Georgia, printed as "Beaswell" in wire reports, on the night of August 25, 1888. He had been accused of "gross immorality" with a Black woman, and an informant told a correspondent that the lynchers were a mixed crowd of white and Black men. Wire dispatches carried the killing to papers as far away as Dakota as a "mysterious lynching."

Braswell was described as a little settlement in the hills at Tunnel, on the East Tennessee, Virginia and Georgia railroad, six miles north of Dallas and forty-two miles from Atlanta. The wire placed it eight miles from Rockmart on the East Tennessee road. According to the Atlanta correspondent of the Savannah Morning News, on the preceding Friday the man went with a Black woman to a hillside near the town and "was openly guilty of gross immorality." When reproached for his conduct, he reportedly said that "he didn't care what they thought about it."

Between 11 and 12 o'clock on Saturday night, a noise was heard on the trestle about 100 yards from the station, and the telegraph operator and night watchman went out to investigate. At the end of the trestle several men stopped them, saying, "This is our business, and will be attended to all right." Out on the high trestle the lynchers tied a rope around the man's neck and threw him over, and the body was left hanging until it was cut down on Sunday morning. In the wire version, the body was discovered by the flagman of a passing train, who saw it hanging from the trestle.
None of the reports named the victim, and no report of an inquest, arrest or charge appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News printed the fullest account on August 28 under the headline "LYNCHED FOR IMMORALITY. Negro Hanged to a Trestle by a Crowd of North Georgians," relaying the accusation and the informant's description without comment. The same day, a short Atlanta dispatch based on a Rockmart telegram appeared in the Wilmington Evening Journal and the Waterbury Evening Democrat as "Mysterious Lynching," stating that the affair was "enveloped in mystery." The Monmouth Inquirer in New Jersey ran the dispatch on August 30.

In Dakota Territory, the Jamestown Weekly Alert and the Mitchell Capital printed the same text under the headline "Only a Negro Lynched." A Daily Republican news summary gave the killing one sentence among accidents and crimes, dating it to Sunday night and adding, "No particulars of the affair are known." Only the Savannah account offered a motive; the wire reports gave no cause and no description of the lynchers.

The Savannah account dated the hanging to Saturday night, between 11 and 12 o'clock, while the Daily Republican summary said Sunday night. The description of the lynchers as "a mixed crowd of white men and negroes" came from a single unnamed informant's "best information," whereas the wire said only that the affair was a mystery.

reader.title: Braswell trestle lynching
bases: A Black man was hanged from a railroad trestle by a group that turned away the station's operator and watchman, on an accusation of immorality (A3); the wire called it a lynching (A2, A6).

A3 reports that 'several parties' described as a 'crowd' tied a rope around the man's neck and threw him from the trestle after he was reproached for 'gross immorality', with no lawful process; the wire independently reports a negro lynched and found hanging from the trestle (A2, A6).

The Savannah Morning News correspondent's account (A3) and the separate Rockmart telegram carried on the wire (A2, A6) agree that a Black man was hanged from a high trestle at Braswell/Beaswell on the East Tennessee road.

accounts.gist: The man was reproached for public immorality on Friday; on Saturday night several men turned back the operator and watchman and threw him from the trestle with a rope around his neck; the lynchers were a mixed crowd of white and Black men.

accounts.label: Wire report (Rockmart telegram via Atlanta)
accounts.gist: A negro was lynched at Beaswell; a train flagman saw the body hanging from a high trestle; the affair was a mystery.

accounts.label: News summary
accounts.gist: A negro was lynched near Rockmart on Sunday night; the body was found by a train flagman; no particulars were known.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headlined 'LYNCHED FOR IMMORALITY. Negro Hanged to a Trestle by a Crowd of North Georgians' and gave the accusation and the informant's account without comment.
Northern dailies ran the Rockmart telegram under 'Mysterious Lynching', stressing that the affair was 'enveloped in mystery'.
Dakota weeklies ran the same telegram under the headline 'Only a Negro Lynched'.
A one-sentence item in a news summary among accidents and crimes, noting that no particulars were known.

conflicts.note: Likely one place: both named versions put it on the East Tennessee railroad; the Savannah account gives the fuller location (six miles north of Dallas, at Tunnel).
